title: Enterprise email classification POC - quant + prompt ops
content:
Purpose and scope:
- Quick notes for the SE-led POC with AcmeCorp (internal name: AcmeMail). Goal: produce a production-feasible pipeline for high-throughput supervised email classification (labels: spam, phishing, priority, auto-route-to-team, triage).
- Focus areas for this doc: model selection rationale, quantization choices (latency vs quality), KV/prefix caching for conversational email threads, prompt templates, and an experiment plan with acceptance criteria.

Constraints and customer context:
- On-premises deployment required for PHI/PII compliance in EU datacenter (customer will run Redwood Private VPC). No data leaves customer's network; model artifacts must be stored on their private repo.
- Peak burst load: ~120 QPS for short messages (avg token length: 60). Tail latency SLO: 95th <= 250ms for request->first-token; overall response complete <= 600ms for classification-only flows.
- Cost sensitivity: they budget for reserved capacity. Want guidance on CPU vs GPU cost tradeoffs and whether 4-bit quantized GPU inference is worthwhile.
- Quality bar: target F1 >= 0.92 on internal test set (balanced across labels); false positives on "phishing" must be minimized.

Baseline model candidates (initial shortlist and why):
- Llama-2-13B-chat (fp16): widely validated, strong NLU; baseline for quality.
- Mistral-Instruct-7B (fp16 / 4-bit): smaller, fast; good for constrained latency but risk on edge-case phishing detection.
- Llama-3-8B or 13B quantized variants: promising tradeoffs for cost + quality.
- Local distilled classifier (small transformer) trained from prompt outputs + labeled data for final fast path (serves as reranker/confirmation).

Selection heuristics we used:
- Prioritize models that maintain precision on rare phishing patterns (we ran a small holdout with 350 labeled adversarial emails).
- If a quantized 7B has >1.5% absolute drop in phishing precision vs fp16 13B baseline, we prefer hybrid cascade (13B fallback).
- Memory fit vs batch sizing: with 16GB A100 equivalent, 4-bit 13B fits with small KV overhead; 8-bit/INT8 options might allow higher concurrency but require more validation.

Quantization plan and notes:
- Experiment 1: GPTQ 4-bit (per-channel) on Llama-2-13B; measure phishing precision, toxicity/overflag behavior, and soft-label calibration drift.
- Experiment 2: PTQ 8-bit/Int8 on Mistral-7B for low-latency path; evaluate mismatch with tokenizer behavior (we saw tokenization boundary divergence in a quick test).
- Calibration step: run 2k representative email samples through fp16 model to collect quantization calibration stats before PTQ/GPTQ.
- KV cache considerations: quantized models show slightly higher KV cache misalignment for long thread context — add a sanity-check to compare per-token logits at context lengths 0/32/128 between fp16 and quantized to detect drift.
- Mixed-precision fallback: keep an fp16 variant in pool as automatic fallback for low-confidence or high-risk inputs (phishing-likely).

Prompt & pipeline design (classification-first cascade):
1) Fast filter: quantized 7B (low-cost) runs classifier prompt that outputs label + confidence. Prompt: concise system message + example few-shot for tricky phishing cues (sender anomalies, embedded links, tokenized URL obfuscation).
2) Reranker/confirm: if confidence in phishing label <0.85 but >0.6, route to 13B fp16 (or 4-bit-13B tested model) with expanded context (last 5 thread emails). 13B returns final decision with an explain field.
3) Deterministic rules: explicit regex checks for well-known patterns (phishing domain list) short-circuit to phishing with high confidence.
4) Final classifier: tiny distilled model (cheap CPU path) for high-throughput non-phishing triage (priority / routing).

Prompt templates (notes):
- Keep examples token-length aware; for quantized 7B we remove long example chains to avoid token overflow.
- Use structured JSON output enforced by a schema to avoid hallucinated labels; e.g. {
  "label": "phishing",
  "confidence": 0.91,
  "explain": "suspicious link: pay-acc+session.example.com"
}
- Add a short post-processing validation step: parse JSON, enforce allowed labels set, clamp confidence range. If parsing fails, escalate to fallback.

Telemetry & evaluation metrics to capture:
- Per-model: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens-per-request, mean CPU/GPU utilization, GPU-memory headroom, errors and timeouts.
- Quality: precision/recall/F1 per label, calibration curve, AUC for phishing class, confusion matrix.
- Cost: estimated tokens/call and monthly token spend baseline vs quantized.
- Operational: frequency of fallback to fp16, parse-failure rate for structured outputs.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Axis A: model (Mistral-7B, Llama-2-13B, Llama-3-8B), Axis B: quant (fp16, 8-bit PTQ, 4-bit GPTQ), Axis C: prompt-length (short / medium / long few-shot).
- Primary measure: phishing precision at 95% recall target. Secondary: 95th latency.
- Run each cell with >=10k samples (stratified by label) if possible; at minimum 2k for early gating.

Operational runbook notes (for SE handoff):
- Deploy model variants as separate routes in Redwood Private: /email-classifier/fast, /email-classifier/rerank, /email-classifier/fallback.
- Route policy: default -> fast; on low-confidence or parse-fail -> rerank; if rerank timeout -> deterministic rules -> final.
- Autoscale considerations: prefer horizontal scaling for 7B fast pool; configure concurrency limits to preserve KV cache locality for 13B fallback.
- Observability: surface per-request model_version, quant_mode, prompt_template_id, and confidence. Hook these into Console dashboards and alerts when fallback rate > 3%.

Unresolved questions / risks:
- GPTQ artifacts: how stable are GPTQ 4-bit weights across subsequent commits? Need to pin quantization toolchain (GitHub PR linked).
- Tokenization drift for non-ASCII email headers: need more samples.
- Regulatory: customer wants proof that no tokens leave VPC — confirm with infra team on Private control-plane guarantees.

Immediate next steps (next 2 weeks):
- Set up reproducible quantization pipeline in our repo (ENG-2318). Owner: Samir.
- Baseline run: fp16 13B on 5k labeled set -> capture metrics. Owner: Avery.
- Run GPTQ 4-bit on 13B with calibration + compare phishing precision on 2k adversarial holdout. Owner: Nadia.
- Build prompt templates (short/medium) and prepare harness to auto-compare structured-output parse rates. Owner: Riley.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we expect a hybrid cascade (fast quantized filter + 13B confirm) to be the likely production architecture for AcmeMail given the phishing precision constraint. If quantized 13B preserves phishing precision within 0.8% of baseline, we can simplify to single-model rollout.
- Please comment on risk-tolerance for fallback rates and whether we should pre-seed a small human-in-the-loop verification set for early production days.

Appendix - quick experiment log (ad-hoc tests run 2025-02-20 to 2025-02-28):
- Quick tokenization check: Mistral tokenizer splits unicode emoji into extra tokens; minor impact on token counts, but safe for classification.
- 200-sample phishing adversarial test: Mistral-7B (fp16) precision 0.87, Llama-2-13B (fp16) precision 0.94.
- GPTQ 4-bit on 13B (single pass): phishing precision dropped to 0.90 — promising but needs calibration.

End of doc.
